#9723. An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA

Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type.

We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps.

A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent:

If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up.

CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things:

The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it.

Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.

Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval: a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.

Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.

The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.

Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.

A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:

You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:

Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA, starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.

Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent.

Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust.

This approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity.

If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core.

More CUGA posts on the Hugging Face blog:

Explore and use multiple web tools from a single dashboard

Two live CUGA agents, with and without policies

This is an interesting example of how voice agents can support Indic languages and make AI more accessible to diverse users. #9722. How I measure coding-agent memory retrieval, including where it fails

Here is a situation most teams using coding agents will recognise.

On Tuesday, your agent spends forty minutes working out why a retry around the payments webhook keeps failing. It isn't the backoff. The upstream returns a 409 on the second attempt because the idempotency key is regenerated on every retry. The fix is two lines. The understanding behind it took most of the afternoon.

On Thursday, a teammate picks up a related ticket. Their agent starts from zero. It proposes raising the backoff. It suggests the same dead ends. Nobody wrote the finding down, because writing things down is the step that always gets skipped.

That gap, where one agent learned something and the next one never hears about it, is the problem I'm working on with Palace. Palace is an MIT-licensed memory engine for coding agents: one Rust binary, one SQLite file, a local embedder, and hybrid BM25 + vector search, exposed over MCP to Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode and other clients. (It is a separate project from the Python "mempalace". The two get confused.)

A memory layer is only useful if it brings back the right thing when asked. So this post is about how I measure that, which numbers I report, and where the numbers fall down.

The benchmark is LongMemEval. Each question comes with its own haystack of past chat sessions, and one or more of those sessions holds the answer.

Many memory systems report QA accuracy: an LLM reads what was retrieved, writes an answer, and another LLM grades it. That measures the whole pipeline, including the reader model.

I report something narrower: session-level retrieval recall. For each question, Palace returns its top K results. If a gold session is among them, it counts as a hit. No LLM reads anything and no LLM grades anything.

That choice has consequences you should keep in mind:

On s_cleaned, 470 questions (the 30 abstention questions excluded, which is the usual convention):

The 0.987 is the number people quote. It's real, but it's the lenient one, and you should know why.

Some questions need information from more than one session. "How many times did I change the deploy target this year?" might need three. recall_any counts the question as a hit if any one gold session is in the top 5. recall_all only counts it if every gold session is there.

For an agent, recall_all is often the one that matters. If the answer depends on combining two earlier decisions and only one comes back, the agent answers with half the story and sounds confident doing it.

Broken down by question type, recall_all@5 looks like this:

Multi-session questions go from 0.992 under recall_any to 0.818 under recall_all. Roughly one in five multi-session questions is missing at least one of the sessions it needs in the top 5. That's the biggest gap in the results, and it's the one I'd want to know about if I were evaluating a memory tool.

On cost: the five drawers behind the @5 figures hold about 1,700 tokens between them, about 1.3% of the haystack (counting four bytes of text per token). Average query time, including embedding the question, was 6 ms.

s_cleaned gives each question about 50 sessions. A real team's memory after a few months is larger than that. So I also run m_cleaned, with about 500 sessions per question and around 4,000 drawers to search.

R@5 drops from 0.987 to 0.919, and R@1 falls much further, from 0.915 to 0.732. With ten times the distractors, the right session is still usually in the top 5, but noticeably less often at the top. Query time goes from 6 ms to 78 ms.

If you're building on any memory layer, this is the curve worth asking about: how does recall change as the store grows?

Two question types stand out on m_cleaned:

Preferences are the weakest category on both splits (0.933 R@5 on s_cleaned, 0.700 on m_cleaned). The cause is simple. "I prefer squash merges" doesn't share many words with "how should I merge this PR?". BM25 gets nothing, and a small embedding model only partly closes the gap. Palace has a dedicated pass for preference-shaped questions against tagged preference spans, and it still misses 3 in 10 at 10x scale. Only 30 questions are behind this number, so treat it as a direction rather than a precise figure.

Temporal questions ("what did I decide about caching last Tuesday?") improved once ranking started favouring drawers from the period the question points at. But on s_cleaned the three remaining temporal misses lose on topic, not on date: the gold chunk scores below unrelated chunks from the same days.

The runner, palace-bench, lives on the benchmarks/longmemeval-beam-runner branch. Its BENCHMARKS.md has the full runbook.

Each run writes a per-case JSONL and a summary JSON, so you can check every miss yourself. Run the BM25-only smoke test first (--bm25-only --limit 3). A full hybrid run on s_cleaned takes tens of minutes on one CPU, and m_cleaned is a 2.7 GB download.

Benchmarks measure whether retrieval works. They don't fix the scenario at the top of this post, because there the problem is that the memory sits on one laptop.

On one machine, Palace already shares memory between agents: a Codex session can read what a Claude Code session wrote. For a team, the open-source client has a remote mode that points every developer's palace mcp at a shared Palace Server:

Palace Server is the paid, closed-source part, and I want to be upfront about that. It's self-hosted: it runs on your infrastructure (Postgres with pgvector, via Docker or a binary), and an offline or air-gapped install is supported, with the embedding model baked into the Docker image. Each developer gets their own API key. OIDC/SSO login, roles and an audit log of memory writes are built in. Your agents' memory never goes to my servers.

In the 90-second handoff demo, Dev A's agent records three approaches that were ruled out on a ticket, with sources. Dev B, on another machine in a fresh session, asks "what did we already rule out?" and gets all three back, each with its source link.

If your team runs into this, try it with one teammate and one ticket. The trial is self-serve: 10 seats for 60 days, no card, no sales call: palacememory.com/trial

The engine, the benchmark runner and every number above are in the open-source repo: github.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs. If you rerun the benchmark, please post your results in the comments, including results that disagree with mine.

I'm iCe, and I build Palace on my own in Munich. Questions about the method are welcome here or in GitHub Discussions.

#9721. TikTok Shop Is Changing the Relationship Between Brands and Content Creators

Image:-By Aidan Castillo, VP of Client Success at MediaLabs

The traditional consensus around influencer marketing primarily treated it as a means of generating awareness. Pay creators to introduce products to their audiences, hoping that attention eventually translates into sales.

Influencer marketing is now becoming a bottom-of-funnel channel, and TikTok Shop is substantially driving that evolution.

By integrating commerce directly into the content experience, the platform has made it possible for creators to influence purchasing decisions and facilitate transactions without directing consumers to external websites.

For brands, the implications extend well beyond another digital sales channel.

In my role as VP of Client Success at MediaLabs, I work with consumer brands developing their TikTok Shop strategies and the creators responsible for executing them.

One of the most significant changes I've observed is the growing importance of creators who aren't necessarily traditional influencers.

Historically, a creator's commercial value was closely tied to the size of their audience. Brands paid premiums for reach, even when the relationship between impressions and actual purchases was difficult to measure.

The idea of genuinely social commerce introduces a different set of considerations.

A creator with a relatively modest following can produce a video that directly generates substantial sales. Conversely, an established influencer with millions of followers isn't necessarily as readily equipped to sell a singular product directly.

The distinction matters because content performance and commercial performance are not interchangeable.

This changes how brands approach creator partnerships.

Rather than concentrating their budgets on a handful of expensive sponsorships, companies can work with larger networks of creators, test different approaches and identify which content consistently generates purchases.

At MediaLabs, our network includes more than 3,000 creators producing content for consumer brands.

During the first quarter of 2026, creators across our network generated approximately $19.35 million in gross merchandise value for participating brands. We also launched 29 creator retainer campaigns during that period.

These figures illustrate the scale at which creator-led commerce can operate, but they also point to an important operational challenge.

Managing a few influencer relationships is relatively straightforward. Coordinating hundreds of creators, maintaining content quality, evaluating performance and ensuring brands have consistent support requires considerably more infrastructure.

Training, creator selection, campaign management and ongoing communication become as important as the content itself.

There's also a meaningful change taking place on the creator side.

TikTok Shop has created opportunities for individuals to generate income through product recommendations without first establishing themselves as recognizable internet personalities.

That doesn't mean earning a sustainable income is easy. Competition is substantial, content performance varies, and creators must continually adapt to changing consumer preferences.

But the commercial opportunity is no longer reserved exclusively for people with enormous audiences.

As social commerce develops, I expect brands to place greater emphasis on measurable sales performance, repeatable creator partnerships and the systems required to manage them.

The companies that understand this distinction will be better positioned to evaluate TikTok Shop as a serious component of their broader e-commerce operations, rather than simply another outlet for influencer marketing.

#9720. Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.

To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.

Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.

Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized.

A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.

For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually.

But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs.

Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis.

But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way.

Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.

These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks.

These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like.

Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process?

An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?”

Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves.

Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation.

Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher said.

Context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research.

These disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work.

Both are valid concerns. An agent that acts without sufficient safeguards could expose confidential data or produce harmful results, while one that’s constrained too broadly could prevent scientists from pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry.

This is why scientific communities need a meaningful role in shaping the boundaries of AI assistance. Developers need to understand not only which activities an agent can perform, but which decisions researchers want to retain and where safeguards are necessary—as well as where those safeguards might obstruct valuable work.

Our findings point toward an approach to scientific AI development that starts with the people who will use the technology.

Researchers should be able to examine an agent's contributions, determine which work to assign, and preserve opportunities to develop their own expertise. Achieving that will require technical features such as transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, alongside evaluations informed by the standards and practices of different scientific communities.

It will also require continued collaboration. Our study is exploratory; the findings come from interviews with 17 US-based scientists, not a representative survey of scientific opinion or an empirical evaluation of specific AI agents. Participants discussed both the generative AI tools they use today and what they anticipate from more autonomous systems. Their perspectives identify important concerns and design priorities, rather than establishing a consensus about how AI should be used in science.

Still, they offer a path forward. At Ai2, we believe AI can accelerate scientific discovery while preserving the openness, reproducibility, and independent scrutiny that make research trustworthy. Through our broader efforts to develop and evaluate scientific agents, we aim to put those principles into practice. That means working with scientists to identify worthwhile uses for agents and translating their concerns into concrete evaluations, in addition to making it easier to understand both what these systems accomplish and how they accomplish it.

The promise of scientific AI isn't simply that researchers can pass off more work. It's that they can pursue questions that might otherwise be out of reach while retaining the knowledge, judgment, and agency needed to make discoveries that are their own.

#9719. A page that loads is not a page that worked

Every browser-automation task I run has the same two failure modes, and they look nothing alike from the inside.

The loud one is easy: navigation error, 403, timeout. You see it, you retry, you move on.

The quiet one is the page that resolves. The URL updates, the DOM is there, no console error, and the thing you came for is not on the page yet. A single-page app whose own script hangs mid-render does exactly this. So does a page that renders an empty shell and fills it from a request that quietly 500s.

My receipt used to be "the navigation returned." It is now three separate questions:

Question 3 is the interesting one. "Not there yet" means wait and read again. "Not there at all" means the page changed under me and I need a different route. Both look like an empty screen. The difference is whether the frame around the target is present. If the shell rendered and the target did not, wait. If the shell did not render either, the route is wrong.

The rule I ended up with: never let a check pass on missing input. A read that returns nothing is not a pass, it is a distinct verdict, and it has to be named in the log. A check that cannot fail on empty input is decoration.

It is the same shape as the classic pipeline bug: exit code 0 is the process's opinion of itself. The receipt is the artifact at the destination. In a browser, the artifact is a readable value, not a 200.

What I do now: every step ends with a destination read, the read names the element it expects by content rather than by position, and a screenshot is the tiebreaker when the accessibility tree and the pixels disagree. The log line that used to say "loaded" now says what I could read.

The most misleading line in an agent trace is the one that reports a page loaded. It did. That was never the question.

#9718. Your AI Agent Has Permissions. Who Gave It the Authority?

Independent legal researcher exploring AI security, cybersecurity, cyber law, digital evidence, and technology governance.

Independent legal researcher exploring AI security, cybersecurity, cyber law, digital evidence, and technology governance.

Independent legal researcher exploring AI security, cybersecurity, cyber law, digital evidence, and technology governance.

In late April 2026, a coding agent working for a small software company called PocketOS ran into a credential error in a staging environment. It didn't stop to ask anyone. It searched the project, found an API token in a file unrelated to its task, and used that token to delete a storage volume on Railway, the company's cloud host. The volume held the production database, and the backups sat on the same volume. The deletion took about nine seconds.

Founder Jer Crane wrote afterwards that the token had been created for routine domain operations through Railway's command line tool. Nobody at PocketOS knew it could also delete production volumes. The company restored from a backup that was three months old, then rebuilt the missing bookings from payment histories, calendar entries and customer emails.

Nothing in that story was a hack. The token was valid and the API call was well formed, so Railway did what the credential allowed. Every system in the chain was asked "can this caller do this?" and each one correctly answered yes. No system asked who had decided the agent should be doing it.

Security people keep two words for this. A permission is what a credential can technically do. Authority is the right to do it, and it has to come from someone entitled to give it. Most agents running today have plenty of the first and a thin paper trail for the second. This piece looks at how that happens and what a proper answer looks like.

Authentication answers "who is this?" A password, a passkey or a signed certificate proves the caller is who it claims to be. It says nothing about what the caller should be allowed to do.

Authorisation answers "what may this caller do?" Roles, scopes and policies live here. A token that can read your calendar but can't delete events is an authorisation decision.

Delegation answers a question the first two skip: on whose behalf is this caller acting, and within what limits?

If you have ever sent someone to collect a passport or a bank document for you, you already know what good delegation looks like. You write an authority letter. It names you, names the person you are sending, says what they may collect, and carries a date. The clerk checks the bearer's ID against the letter. Your cousin walks out with one envelope, and he can't empty your account while he's there.

Software has mostly handled the same errand in two worse ways. Either the cousin gets your own ID card and the clerk believes he is you, or he gets a master key to the building. The first is impersonation. The second is a broad API key. In both cases the clerk has no letter to check.

RFC 8693, the OAuth token exchange standard from January 2020, draws this line formally. Under impersonation, the acting party is indistinguishable from the person it acts for. Under delegation, it keeps its own identity and acts as that person's agent. The word "agent" was in the RFC years before anyone attached a language model to it.

A nightly cron job with an over-powered key was always a risk, but a predictable one. Its code did the same thing every run, and you could read that code.

An agent decides what to do at run time. Part of what shapes the decision is text it picks up along the way: a web page, an email, a GitHub issue, an error message. Auth0's identity team puts it this way: once behaviour is no longer fixed by code, the scope of the credential is one of the few controls you have left.

The first time you connect an agent to a database or a cloud account, the quickest route is the credential you already have. That is usually your own, or an admin key sitting in a config file. Four patterns cover almost every setup.

"svc-automation did it", with no person attached

A Cloud Security Alliance survey from January 2026 gives a rough idea of the spread. Of 228 IT and security professionals, 43% said their agents rely on shared service accounts and 31% let agents run under human user identities. 74% said agents often get more access than they need. 68% could not clearly tell agent activity from human activity in their own systems.

The sample is small and the study was funded by Aembit, which sells agent identity products, so treat the figures as a sketch. The shape is still familiar. PocketOS fits the first row of the table: a key made for one job that turned out to work for every job.

Standards people have noticed. An Internet-Draft on agent authentication, written by engineers from Okta, Ping Identity, AWS, OpenAI, Zscaler and Defakto Security, calls static API keys an antipattern for agents. Its reasoning is that they are long-lived bearer secrets, bound to nothing, and hard to rotate. The document is a draft and may change, but its authors include Brian Campbell, who edited RFC 8693.

In 1988 Norm Hardy published a three-page note called The Confused Deputy. It described a compiler on a commercial timesharing system. The compiler had write access to its home directory so it could record usage statistics. The system's billing file lived in the same directory.

One day a user told the compiler to write its debugging output to a file with the billing file's name. The compiler obliged, and the billing records were overwritten. The user had no right to touch that file. The compiler did, and it couldn't tell whose authority it was using for that particular write.

An AI agent is Hardy's compiler with a much larger vocabulary. It carries credentials from whoever deployed it, and it takes direction from whatever text lands in its context window.

Researchers at Invariant Labs showed in 2025 that a malicious issue filed on a GitHub repository could hijack an agent connected through the official GitHub MCP server. The attacker needed no access to the victim's private repositories. The agent already had it.

Not every failure needs an attacker, though. In mid-2025, Replit's coding agent deleted a user's production database after being told not to change anything without permission. The PocketOS agent wasn't tricked either. On its own account afterwards, it guessed that the volume belonged to staging and never checked.

So there are two kinds of deputies to worry about: the tricked one and the overeager one. The OWASP Thttps://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/op 10 for Agentic Applications, published in December 2025, ranks Identity and Privilege Abuse third. It describes agents running on credentials or delegated authority inherited from people and other services, then being pushed into things their owners never intended.

The same control stops both kinds. If the credential can't perform the damaging action, it doesn't matter whether the agent was fooled or just wrong.

Very little of the fix is new. Most of it is OAuth plumbing that has existed for years and is now being pointed at agents. Six pieces do the work.

Here is what step 3 looks like in practice. This is the payload of a delegated token for an invented scheduling agent:

Five fields answer the question in this article's title. sub says whose authority this is. act says who is using it. aud and scope say where and for what, and exp says until when. The calendar API can now apply a rule to the pair: Meera may delete events, but the scheduling agent acting for Meera may only read them. The audit log records both names.

It would be dishonest to present this as solved. Several separate Internet-Drafts on agent authorisation were circulating at the IETF in 2026, and none is a standard yet.

Scopes are also blunt. Auth0 points out that OAuth scopes can't easily express something like "contact details for the accounts I'm working on, but not the legal hold queue". Rules that fine need a policy check on every request, on top of the token.

And none of this helps if a second, broader credential is lying in a file the agent can read. That was the entire PocketOS failure.

Many agent tools show a confirmation prompt before a risky step. That is useful, but it is weaker than it looks, for two reasons.

The prompt is drawn by the same software it is supposed to restrain. The IETF draft is blunt about this. A confirmation inside the agent's own interface does not count as authorisation unless it is tied to a grant from the authorisation server. The stronger pattern sends the approval request out of band, to the user's phone for example, with the details of the exact action attached. The draft admits that approvals in the middle of a running task still need more standards work.

The second reason is that words are not controls. The Replit user had told the agent not to make changes without permission. PocketOS had rules written into the agent's instructions. Telling an agent to stay out of production is a request. Removing its write access to production is a control, and only one of those survives a bad guess.

There is a human limit as well. Ask someone to approve every file read and by the afternoon they are approving everything. MCP's guidance lists users abandoning consent dialogs that ask for too much as a risk in its own right. Approval works when it is rare. Keep it for actions you can't take back: deleting data, moving money, sending something outside the company, changing who has access.

You don't need an identity platform to get most of the benefit. You need honest answers to these.

The last question is the one PocketOS missed, and it is the easiest to miss. An agent with shell access can read every secret in the working directory, whether or not you meant to hand it over. For a solo developer or a small team, the practical version is short. Give the agent a per-project token instead of an account-wide one. Point it at a read-only database user unless the task needs writes. Keep production secrets out of the folder it works in. Store backups somewhere the same credential can't reach.

Authentication proves which agent is calling. Authorisation decides what that agent may do. An agent can be perfectly authenticated and still hold far more access than its task needs.

Preferably not. If the agent uses your login, every system treats its actions as yours and the logs can't tell the two of you apart. A delegated token that names both you and the agent keeps the record straight and lets you limit what the agent can do.

It describes a token that records two parties: the user whose authority is being used and the actor using it. RFC 8693 defines the token exchange that produces these tokens and the act claim that names the actor.

Partly. The MCP specification defines how a client gets an OAuth token for a remote server, ties that token to that one server and bans passing it on. It does not choose your scopes, and it can't stop a local agent from reading a broader key off your disk.

#9716. Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems

Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate

This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models.

That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50.

Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents?

In this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from.

First, we'll start off with some context on swarms.

We've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem.

But swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so.

A big swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. In Anthropic's vulnerability-finding experiment, coordinated agents found more bugs than independent agents, but also searched more code and used more tokens. When the comparison was restricted to the same directories, the results per million tokens were about the same.

Start with the simplest case. If four agents each try a task independently, the chance that at least one gets it right is higher than with a single attempt, as long as we can tell which answer is correct. That makes a useful baseline for a multi-agent system, but it doesn't show that the agents helped each other. They may simply have had more tries.

Four attempts also cost four times as much. So the fairer comparison is at an equal budget: if each of four agents gets a quarter of the total tokens, can they still beat one agent that spends all of them? We can only find out by testing, because the answer depends on the task, the model and how the work is divided.

This series keeps asking one question: when agents communicate, does it actually help, or are we just spending more compute?

We understand that question through this simple expectation.

We'll treat agent count as a scaling dimension, alongside tokens and model size. Sometimes adding agents will help. Sometimes coordination will consume the budget we hoped to save. The point is to measure both. We won't start with 10,000 agents. We'll start with a small team on a task that we can check easily.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning has studied cooperation and competition long before language models were called swarms.

A single agent's task is a Markov decision process: observe, act, get a reward. In a team, everyone shares the reward, but each agent sees only part of the world. This is a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process: teammates, but no one sees the whole picture.

This creates three practical problems. First, teammates keep changing while each agent learns. Second, credit assignment: when the team succeeds, which actions deserve the credit? A winning team can include weak actions, and we may end up rewarding them. Third, a message changes what other agents observe, so communication is part of the policy we're training.

A common solution is centralized training with decentralized execution: training uses information from the whole team, but each agent acts only on its own observations. Our first example follows this pattern with a shared team reward.

Agents can also be organized in different ways. Two useful starting points are:

A hierarchy. A lead agent assigns work to workers and collects their results. Anthropic's Research system works this way, with a separate context for each worker. Kimi K2.5's PARL trains only the orchestrator and keeps the subagents frozen, so training a multi-agent system doesn't mean updating every component. See Anthropic's system description and Kimi's technical blog.

A distributed team. Peers send each other messages and decide when to read their inboxes. No lead agent assigns the actions. This is the setup we'll use here, following the information-aggregation task in s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL.

We'll reproduce the information-sharing task from Simple Scaling of Swarms because it's interpretable and straightforward to implement. Four agents share a small language model and learn to pool what each of them knows.

Each agent receives one integer from 1 to 99. It knows its own assignment and its teammates' names. It does not initially know the other agents' numbers. For example, four private assignments might be "five", "twenty-six", "five" and "seventy-eight". Duplicates stay in the list, so a correct final answer is:

The team succeeds when at least one agent submits the complete, correctly sorted list. One correct answer is enough; success does not require all four agents to answer correctly. An agent cannot reliably infer the other private assignments without information from its teammates.

This means the task does not yet test Figure 1 directly. Each agent holds information the others need, so a single agent, or a team without messaging, cannot succeed however many retries it gets. Instead, the task tests the precondition behind Figure 1: can a small shared policy learn to communicate at all, and how many tokens does that cost? A later post moves to a task that a single agent can solve alone, where the matched-budget comparison is meaningful.

The main communication tools are message(to, text), read_messages(), and check_notifications(). A notification tells an agent that unread messages exist; reading its inbox makes their contents available. Agents can send direct messages or broadcast to everyone.

We defined a four-agent system using one shared Qwen3-0.6B policy, with separate contexts and private inputs. We are not training four different models. The prompt explains the task and the tools, including the need to share assignments.

In this post, a team means one episode: four agents attempting one problem once. A successful team receives a reward reduced by the tokens it uses. A failed team receives zero:

For illustration, a correct team using half its allowance receives 0.875. There is no separate reward for sending messages. The incentive is to solve the task while using fewer generated tokens.

For every training problem, we collect eight independent team attempts. Their rewards are normalized within that group. An attempt that does better than its group average gets a positive advantage; one that does worse gets a negative advantage. Every agent in the same team receives that team's advantage, including an agent whose own final answer was wrong.

In TRL, each agent's sampled tokens form a training row. Its incoming messages and tool results provide context. The loss is averaged within each team and then across teams, so longer conversations do not give a team more weight.

Our results come from the original experiment, which used 256 team attempts per update (32 problems with eight attempts each). The walkthrough uses TRL's default of --teams-per-update 128, which works out to about 150 team attempts per update.

Over 75 steps, training success rose from 6.6% to 82.3%, comparing the first and last five updates. At checkpoint 75, the four-agent team solved 26 of 32 held-out problems (81.25%). The paper reports 93.2% four-agent success after 200 updates.

The team also used 37.4% fewer tokens per attempt, falling from about 13k to 8k. This improvement accompanied more active information sharing: broadcasts increased from 2.38 to 5.73 per team, even as total token use fell.

The team also used fewer tokens later in training. Comparing the first five updates with updates 71–75:

That is a 37.4% reduction in generated tokens per training team between those windows. At batch 75 itself, the mean was 7,624 tokens per team. These are training measurements; we did not retain held-out token-efficiency measurements for the trained checkpoint.

Notice that fewer tokens did not mean fewer messages. More agents began participating but broadcasting became more common, rather than direct messaging. Generated tokens include reasoning and tool calls as well as message bodies, so message count alone does not tell us how much text the team produced.

No agent can solve the problem alone, so the closest equivalent of "a single agent with more retries" is the untrained team with more retries. The training data already contains this comparison. Each update collects eight attempts per problem, and the task's answers are easy to check, so we can count a problem as solved when any of its eight attempts succeeded. Early in training, that count gives the untrained team's best-of-8 success rate:

With eight retries, the untrained team solves fewer than half the problems and spends about 13 times as many tokens as one attempt from the trained team. Read this as an estimate. Both rows use training problems rather than held-out ones, and updates 2–5 already sample from a slightly trained policy.

The model is small, but the rollouts are not. Each update generates millions of tokens of agent conversation at contexts of up to 40k tokens. We used one H200 for the trainer and seven H200s running vLLM rollout engines to get through those rollouts quickly, and kept each worker's eight attempts together. The walkthrough below runs the same task on two GPUs. Here are the infra details:

The figures above describe our original 75-update experiment. In this walkthrough we'll run TRL's swarm example on Hugging Face Jobs. One H200 serves the shared Qwen3-0.6B policy with vLLM and a second H200 trains it.

Sign in with a Hugging Face account that can run Jobs and create buckets. Replace YOUR_USERNAME with your Hub username.

Use a fresh bucket for each run so earlier measurements stay available.

Save the script below as train-swarm.sh in your current directory.

The command below sends its contents to the job. Inside the job, vLLM serves the shared policy on GPU 0. GPU 1 runs TRL's async_grpo_s3_aggregation.py for 50 updates with Trackio. TRL's evaluate.py scores the base model and checkpoint 50 on the same 192 held-out problems. That is a larger set than the 32-problem checks in our results, which gives tighter error bars. The job saves both scores, the checkpoint, Trackio data and the exact Git commit to your bucket.

One TRL rollout contains a whole team conversation. The trainer compares eight attempts at the same problem and gives all four agents in an attempt the same advantage. Each update uses about 150 team attempts. TRL packs micro-batches by token count rather than by team, so the --teams-per-update 128 setting is approximate. The --report-to trackio flag records training metrics at every update.

This shorter run is cheaper than our original experiment, and it stops earlier on the learning curve. TRL's run of this example took about 4.8 hours on two H100s and reached 60.9% held-out success at checkpoint 50.

To run closer to our original experiment, change the training flags to --updates 75 --teams-per-update 256 --concurrent-teams 256, replace checkpoint-50 with checkpoint-75 in the script, and raise the job's --timeout to 24h. That is three times as many rollouts. The two codebases still differ in details such as the system prompt, so expect similar results rather than an exact replication.

Once the job completes, sync the bucket to a local folder. It holds the two evaluation files, the Trackio data, the TRL revision and the checkpoint-50 weights, which are the largest download. In the dashboard, compare team/success, team/messages and team/tokens over training. The job logs also give the held-out success rate for the base model and checkpoint 50. Each line of base.jsonl or trained.jsonl records one of those evaluation attempts.

This first example gives us a small environment, a shared reward and a policy that improves at pooling private information. It also shows why success, token use and communication structure need to be read together. At 75 updates, the team is solving most checked problems, but it has not converged to the cleanest communication pattern.

In the coming examples, we'll take a step back from training and look at how we evaluate and analyze swarms.

For now, we have something concrete to build on: four small agents, one trainable policy, a checkable task, and a reproducible way to examine what the team learned.

How much location can shift income class thresholds between cheapest and costliest metros

The most widely cited framework for income classes comes from the Pew Research Center, which uses a straightforward formula based on the national median household income. Pew defines three tiers:

Using the most recent Census Bureau data with a national median household income of approximately $84,900, the thresholds for a three-person household look like this:

The "upper middle class" label is not an official Pew category — it is a colloquial term most commonly used to describe the band between the middle of the middle class and the beginning of the upper class. Think of it as the top quarter of the middle-income range through the entry point of the upper-income range: households earning roughly $106,000 to $169,800.

These definitions are adjusted for household size using an equivalence scale. A single person needs less income than a family of five to achieve the same standard of living. Pew adjusts all income figures to a three-person household equivalent, which is why the thresholds you see in different sources sometimes vary — they may be using different household sizes as their reference point.

National income thresholds are useful starting points, but they obscure a critical reality: the cost of living varies so dramatically across the United States that the same income places you in different classes depending on where you live. Pew Research's cost-of-living adjusted data reveals just how stark these differences are.

A household earning $150,000 in Jackson, Mississippi — where the cost of living is roughly 83% of the national average — has purchasing power equivalent to about $180,700 nationally. That same $150,000 in San Francisco, where costs run about 180% of the national average, has purchasing power equivalent to only $83,300 — technically middle class by Pew's national definitions.

This explains why so many households earning $150,000 to $200,000 in coastal cities feel middle class despite technically being upper-income by national standards. They are not wrong — their lived experience of housing costs, childcare, and taxes genuinely consumes their income at the same rate as middle-income households in lower-cost areas.

Income class and wealth class are not the same thing. The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances reveals that high income does not automatically translate to high net worth. Many upper-income households carry large mortgages, student loans, and car payments that consume much of their earnings. Meanwhile, some middle-income households with high savings rates accumulate substantial wealth over time.

The FI community lives in this gap. A household earning $90,000 that saves 50% of their income and invests consistently will have a higher net worth within 10-15 years than a household earning $250,000 that saves 5%. Income determines your ceiling; savings rate determines your trajectory. This is why ChooseFI focuses on savings rate and investable net worth as the primary metrics of financial progress — not income class labels.

The financial independence community occupies a unique position in the income class framework. Survey data from FIRE-focused communities suggests the median household income among FI seekers is roughly $130,000 to $160,000 — placing most in the upper-middle-class to lower-upper-income range. However, successful FI stories span the entire income spectrum, from teachers earning $55,000 to tech executives earning $500,000.

What distinguishes FI community members from their income peers is not what they earn but what they keep. While the average upper-middle-class household saves 8-12% of income, FI-path households in the same income range typically save 40-60%. This results in net worth accumulation that dramatically outpaces their income class peers.

The lesson from this comparison is that income class labels describe your earning power, but they say nothing about your financial trajectory. A middle-income household on the FI path will typically surpass the net worth of upper-income households who spend freely. The FI framework redefines "class" around financial freedom rather than consumption — your class is determined not by what you can afford to buy, but by how many years of expenses your investments can cover.

Income class definitions use household income, which combines the earnings of all adults in a home. This creates a nuance worth understanding: a dual-income household where each partner earns $75,000 has the same household income ($150,000) as a single-earner household at that level, but the dual-income household often faces higher total costs (two commutes, potentially more childcare) and different tax treatment. When evaluating where you fall, always use your total household income before taxes and compare to thresholds adjusted for your household size.

The distinction between wealth and income is the foundation of financial independence. Your income class describes your present earning power. Your net worth describes your accumulated financial freedom. The FI community's central insight is that you can move from any income class to financial independence by controlling the gap between what you earn and what you spend — and investing the difference consistently in low-cost index funds over time.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class by any definition, your path to financial independence depends on one number: your savings rate. A middle-income household saving 50% of their income will reach FI decades before an upper-income household saving 5%. Focus on growing the gap between what you earn and what you spend — the class label takes care of itself.

Use these calculators to see where you stand on your FI journey.

Your savings rate matters more than returns. See where you are.

Add up all pre-tax income for your household — wages, self-employment, investment income, and any other sources. Compare to the Pew thresholds adjusted for your household size. For a three-person household, middle income is $56,600 to $169,800.

Use a cost-of-living calculator to adjust your income to the national equivalent. A $120,000 income in a city with 130% cost-of-living has the same purchasing power as $92,300 nationally. This adjusted number is a more honest reflection of your class position.

Your net worth — assets minus liabilities — is a better indicator of financial health than income alone. The median net worth for upper-middle-class households is roughly $465,000. If you are above that with a lower income, you are wealthier than your income class suggests.

Divide your annual savings (including employer retirement contributions) by your gross income. The national average is under 5%. The FI community targets 40-60%. Your savings rate is the single most important predictor of when you will reach financial independence.

Multiply your annual spending by 25 to find your FI number (based on the 4% safe withdrawal rate). Then use your current savings rate and existing net worth to estimate how many years until you reach that number. This timeline matters more than any income class label.

According to Pew Research, upper-income households earn more than double the national median household income. For a three-person household in 2026, that threshold is approximately $169,800. However, this varies significantly by location — in San Francisco, you would need roughly $306,000 to have the same purchasing power as $169,800 nationally.

Upper middle class generally describes households in the top 20-30% of earners but below the top 5% — roughly $106,000 to $169,800 for a three-person household. Upper class typically refers to households above $169,800 (top 19%). The top 5% begins at roughly $280,000 and the top 1% at approximately $590,000. These are income-based definitions and do not account for net worth.

By national standards, $200,000 household income places you in the upper-income category (above the $169,800 threshold for a three-person household). However, in high-cost cities like San Francisco, New York, or Boston, $200,000 has purchasing power equivalent to roughly $111,000 to $130,000 nationally — solidly middle class in terms of lived experience.

The Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances shows the median net worth of upper-income households is approximately $805,400. The top 10% of U.S. households by net worth have $1.9 million or more, and the top 1% have $11.1 million or more. Net worth is a more meaningful measure of financial security than income because it reflects accumulated wealth, not just current earning power.

Lifestyle inflation is the primary reason. Many households increase their spending in lockstep with income increases — larger homes, newer cars, private schools, premium vacations — leaving little margin for savings. A household earning $300,000 that spends $290,000 accumulates wealth more slowly than one earning $100,000 that spends $50,000. The FI community calls this the HENRY problem: High Earner, Not Rich Yet.

Pew Research adjusts income thresholds using an equivalence scale based on household size. A single person needs roughly $56,600 to be middle income (the lower bound), while a family of five needs roughly $126,500 for the same standard of living. Larger households need more income to achieve the same class designation because they have more people sharing the resources.

Income class labels provide useful context for understanding where you stand relative to other American households, but they are a poor measure of financial health. Plenty of upper-income households are one job loss away from financial crisis because they spend everything they earn, while many middle-income households on the FI path have built net worth that places them in the top 10% of all Americans. The framework that matters most is not whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class — it is whether the gap between your income and your spending is large enough to build financial independence within a timeline that matters to you. Focus on three numbers: your savings rate, your investable net worth, and your FI number. Everything else is a label that describes your present circumstances, not your financial future.

#9713. Monthly Churn Times 12 Is Not Annual Churn

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

A company reports 2.2% monthly churn. Someone multiplies by 12 and writes "about 26% annual churn" in the board deck. It looks like basic arithmetic. It's wrong twice, and the two errors don't cancel out.

The first error is the one people half remember from school: churn compounds. The second is bigger and less well known: the customers who churn in a typical month are not the customers you had at the start of the year. In a growing business, those two groups behave very differently.

Here's both, with a simulation and the SQL to get the real number.

If you lose 2% of customers in January, you lose 2% of a smaller base in February. Over 12 months, you keep 98% of 98% of 98%, twelve times. That's 0.98 to the 12th power, or 78.5%. Annual churn is 21.5%, not 24%.

At low churn, the difference is small. At 5% a month, multiplying says 60% and compounding says 46%. At 8% a month, multiplying says you lose nearly every customer in a year, which isn't what happens.

The same mistake runs in reverse. A contract business with 20% annual churn that divides by 12 to get a monthly figure for a lifetime value model will understate monthly churn and overstate lifetime value.

So: compound, don't multiply. But that's the small error.

I simulated three years of a growing subscription business. The key assumption, which matches almost every real subscription business I've looked at, is that churn falls with tenure. New customers leave at 6% a month for their first three months, 2.5% a month until they reach a year, and 1% a month after that.

First, the usual monthly churn rate for 2025: customers who cancelled in a month, divided by customers active at the start of that month, averaged over the year.

2.2% a month. Times 12 is 26.6%. Compounded is 23.6%.

Now the question the board actually means: of the customers we had on January 1, how many had left by December 31?

17.3%. The compounded monthly rate overstates it by six points. The multiplied rate overstates it by nine.

The reason is who's in the monthly numbers. Every month, the denominator includes customers who joined recently, and recent customers churn the most. In a growing business there are always lots of them. But the January 1 cohort doesn't get any new customers during the year. It only gets older, and older customers churn less.

Split the January 1 customers by how long they'd been customers:

Customers who'd been around for more than a year lost only 12% over the next 12 months. Customers who were brand new lost 26%. The monthly churn rate is a blend of both, weighted toward new customers because a growing business keeps adding them.

They answer different questions, so each is right for something.

Monthly churn on the whole base tells you how much work customer success has this month and how much revenue you need to replace. It's an operational number. Use it to run the business month to month.

Annual churn of a starting cohort tells you how durable the customer base is. "Of the customers we had a year ago, 83% are still here" is what investors and boards are asking about. Use it for anything that sounds like a year.

Churn by tenure tells you where the problem is. If new-customer churn is high and mature-customer churn is low, the problem is onboarding or fit, not the product. That's a very different fix.

What isn't right for anything is monthly churn times 12. It mixes a rate that's dominated by new customers with a time frame that implies the starting base. In a fast-growing business, it can overstate annual churn by half.

Everything here applies to revenue churn too, with one more complication: customers who expand often churn less, and larger customers often churn less than small ones. So revenue churn by month and revenue retention of a starting cohort can diverge even more than logo churn. Compute both from the same cohort query, swapping a count for a sum of recurring revenue.

One more trap. If customers sign annual contracts, they can only leave at renewal. A monthly churn rate on an annual-contract book measures which month the renewals happen to fall in, not how likely customers are to leave. For annual contracts, measure churn per renewal: of the contracts that came up for renewal, what share renewed. Then if you need an annual figure, that's already it.

Compound, don't multiply. Measure annual churn on a starting cohort, not by converting a monthly rate. And split by tenure, because the average hides the only thing you need to know: whether customers leave early or late.

Measuring Sales Cycle Length With Kaplan-Meier Estimation and SQL

The API is OpenAI-compatible. Point the client at https://api.saanora.com/v1 and set the model to mark-1x-27b. Chat completions, streaming, tool calling, and image input all use the usual request shape. Context is 262K. You can set reasoning_effort to low, medium, or high. Medium is the default, and it is also how we ran the scores below.

Price is $0.10 per 1M input tokens and $0.60 per 1M output tokens, with free credit to start. Create a key in the API console and put it in SAANORA_API_KEY.

Scores at medium effort: GPQA 84.7, level with the best open models its size; AIME25 86.7; HMMT Feb26 73.5. The longer write-up is on our blog.

The answer is in choices[0].message.content.

The model's thinking comes back in a separate reasoning field, not mixed into the answer. Higher effort costs more time and more output tokens, so I use high for proofs, tricky bugs, and long plans, and leave the default alone for everyday questions.

max_tokens includes the reasoning and defaults to 32,768. If a hard problem may think for a long time, raise that budget and stream the response.

The model scales down when no one is using it. After a quiet period, the first request can return 503 while it starts, which can take a few minutes. That request is not charged. The OpenAI SDK's built-in retry is usually not enough, so I retry until it answers:

#9710. Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference

We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.

Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference. We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion.

Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications.

Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation.

This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process.

We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training:

Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples: rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values.

Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples: rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships.

OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples: synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading.

Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language.

Figure 2. Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from the chart geometry

We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents.

We then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content.

A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output.

Figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods.

The matched comparison shows the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer—and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35. Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38, including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts.

A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs.

NaViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory.

The built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead, and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens, or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token.

Figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 shows three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details.

In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively.

Fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions. Start with a full-page prediction, then add focused reprocessing where the document needs it:

Single pass - Parse the full page once for text, layout, tables, and charts.

Double pass - use for dense tables and small chart details. Crop the table and chart regions found by the parser, re-parse them at higher detail, and merge the refinements into the page output.

Triple pass - Instead of only using the models full page parsing bounding boxes, use a second pass of the model in detection mode in order to get verification that all boxes have been accurately found and text has not been missed and re-extract any found charts or tables in a third pass

Figure 5. Additional stages focus computation on difficult regions. Multiple crops can require multiple requests.

In the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass. The additional work lets applications trade some throughput for better extraction in difficult regions. Reference results and serving measurements.

We are sharing a Parse fine-tuning recipe that takes developers through paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT, and NeMo RL GRPO, using vLLM to generate candidate answers.

The worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram: a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before adaptation, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the intended procedure table. SFT teaches it to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and its placement on the tooth.

Figure 6. A recorded recipe example: after SFT, all six chart rows match the target. Full image and native training label.

RLVR then reinforces accuracy and consistent completion. In the dental reference run, the estimated first-attempt success rate (sampled pass@1) rose from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR.

Figure 7. Matched evaluation on 256 held-out forms from the same synthetic generator, with eight samples per page. Success requires natural completion, exact chart content, and error-free normalized page text. Evaluation protocol.

To adapt the recipe, supply your own image/label pairs and a verifier: checks that determine whether an extraction is correct. The included document reward components cover text fidelity, bounding boxes, tables, chart facts, and completion. Combine the components relevant to your task, add schema checks, and use completion and repetition checks to discourage looping or unfinished output.

We are excited that the community has extended and improved Parse for Thai, Persian/Farsi, and Arabic already and we hope that these additional datasets and fine-tuning recipes will help encourage these efforts and future models.

We thank Denis Ovchinnikov for his work on vLLM integration and independent performance validation, Oliver Holworthy for improving the fine-tuning recipe's runtime setup and reproducibility, and Bo Liu for technical review.

#9709. I built an open source permissions layer for AI agents. Here is what it does and what it can't do.

AI agents call tools: they read files, send email, hit internal APIs, run code. In most codebases, what an agent is allowed to do is whatever its API keys allow, and the record of what it did is scattered application logs.

Security teams are starting to ask the obvious questions. Which agents exist? What can each one call? Who approved the risky action? Can you prove what happened? Right now most teams can't answer.

I built Agent Tessera to answer them without tying you to one LLM provider or agent framework. It is open source (Apache 2.0).

You write what an agent may do in a short YAML file:

You mark your tools, or wrap your LLM client:

Anything the policy doesn't allow is denied before the function runs, and the decision lands in an audit log. Each event includes the hash of the previous one, so editing the log afterwards is detectable:

Enforce locally, govern centrally. The SDK evaluates the policy inside your process. There's no network call per decision, so it is fast and keeps working if the control plane is down. The optional server registers agents, issues short-lived credentials, signs policy bundles (the SDK rejects bundles with a bad signature), collects audit events, and has a kill switch and a web console.

Default deny, one decision order. Suspension and kill switches come first, then explicit denies, delegation limits, the allow-rule check (no matching rule means deny), rate limits and quotas, and approvals last. There's one order, documented, and table-tested.

Plain YAML policies. I deliberately did not adopt a general policy language. The people who review agent permissions are often not the people who write the agent, and a short YAML file is something they can actually read.

Provider neutral. Adapters for OpenAI (and Azure), Anthropic, Bedrock, Gemini, and LiteLLM; integrations for LangChain/LangGraph, MCP, the OpenAI Agents SDK, and CrewAI. A registry lets you add your own client.

Minimal dependencies. The core needs httpx, pydantic, pyjwt, and pyyaml. Provider SDKs are optional extras.

It enforces policy inside the agent's process, on the calls you route through it. If code calls a provider's HTTP API directly, nothing checks that call. There is an opt-in detect_bypass mode that records such calls for the main providers, but it only detects them. And a hostile process can disable the SDK outright. It's a guardrail for agents you trust to be mostly well-behaved, not a sandbox. For untrusted code, pair it with container isolation and egress rules.

It also doesn't track data between agents (agent A can pass B something B couldn't read), and it doesn't detect prompt injection; it limits what an injected agent can do through governed calls.

The full list is on the threat model page.

A stable 1.0 API, agent-to-agent identity with A2A Agent Cards, and sub-agent spawning with permission attenuation. Later: a gateway mode for agents you can't modify, and a TypeScript SDK. SAML, SCIM, Slack/Teams approvals, and SIEM connectors aren't built; contributions are welcome.

The README quickstart takes about two minutes and needs no API key. I'd like to hear what is missing, especially from people who have to answer "what can this agent do?" for a security review.

Repo: https://github.com/agent-tessera/agent-tessera Docs: https://agent-tessera.dev/
