#9707. Row Counts Won’t Save Your Cutover

Recognized data engineering expert and thought leader with more than 16years of experience architecting large-scale enterprise data platform

Recognized data engineering expert and thought leader with more than 16years of experience architecting large-scale enterprise data platform

Recognized data engineering expert and thought leader with more than 16years of experience architecting large-scale enterprise data platform

A reconciliation-first approach to CDC into Redshift, and where GoldenGate and AWS DMS pipelines actually go wrong.

Cutover night. The row counts match to the last digit. Somebody posts a green checkmark in the channel and everyone goes to bed.

Three days later, finance asks why order totals for one region are off by a few thousand dollars. Nothing is down. Nothing alerted. The counts still match. That’s the problem.

The pattern is familiar to anyone who has moved a busy database onto a new platform. The pipeline gets built, the full load finishes, change data capture (CDC) hums along, and the team picks the one check that’s easy to run: count the rows. Counts catch missing data. They say nothing about data that arrived wrong, arrived twice, or never got its update.

This article is about the checks I’d automate before trusting either GoldenGate or AWS DMS to feed Redshift, and the lag arithmetic that tells you when the pipeline is falling behind.

Every number below comes from one worked example with made-up data: an Oracle ORDERS table of 480 million rows being replicated into Redshift. It is illustrative, not from a real system, and I flag it each time.

A matching count proves the pipeline didn’t lose or duplicate whole rows at one moment in time. It’s a useful first check, and I run it. But look at what it can’t see:

An update was lost or applied out of order

Counts drift, but only after enough deletes

A large text column was truncated in flight

An empty string became NULL (or the reverse)

Timestamps lost precision or shifted time zone

Five of those six defects leave the count untouched or only occasionally move it. If your exit criterion is “counts match,” you’ve certified the easiest thing to get right.

People compare GoldenGate and DMS on feature lists. I compare them on what happens when something goes wrong, because that’s where the weekends go. This is my rule of thumb, not a law. Check licensing and the current documentation for your versions before you decide.

Extract reads the redo, writes trail files

A task on a replication instance reads the source logs

Trail files absorb the backlog (size the disk)

Source logs must stay available until the task catches up

High-volume Oracle estates, strict ordering, long-lived replication

Time-boxed migrations, small teams, AWS-native stacks

Whichever you choose, the target side looks the same, and that’s where most of this article lives.

The pipeline is easy to draw. The discipline is in giving each stage a check that can fail loudly:

I land every change as an append-only record with its operation, commit position and sequence. Then I apply only the latest change per key. Two reasons. First, retries and replays are harmless, because applying the same batch twice gives the same result. Second, Redshift doesn’t enforce primary keys. They’re informational, used by the planner, so the target will happily store duplicates and won’t tell you.

Untested sketch, Redshift SQL (check syntax against your cluster version; newer clusters also support MERGE):

Deletes arrive as a change record, so the DELETE removes the old row and the INSERT skips it. Updates become delete-plus-insert, which suits a columnar store far better than row-by-row updates. In the worked example, 12 million changes a day split into 6.6 million inserts, 4.8 million updates and 0.6 million deletes (55%, 40% and 5%). Batching those is not optional.

Average lag is a comfortable lie. Here’s the arithmetic for the example. The table sees 12 million changes a day, about 139 a second on average and roughly 1,100 a second in the busiest hour (I assumed an 8x peak). Suppose the apply side can sustain 3,000 changes a second. That’s 2.7 times the peak. Healthy.

Now somebody runs a backfill that updates 40 million rows in an hour. That adds about 11,100 changes a second, for a total near 11,250 against capacity of 3,000. The surplus is 8,250 a second.

Using lag ≈ backlog ÷ apply rate as a rough estimate, a 5-minute target is breached after about 109 seconds, because the backlog passes 900,000 changes. By the end of the job the backlog is 29.7 million and lag peaks near 165 minutes. Draining it at the 2,861 a second of headroom takes another 173 minutes, so the pipeline is back to normal about 293 minutes after the job started.

A backfill that takes an hour at the source can cost you five hours of staleness downstream.

Two habits fix most of this. Alert when lag is rising for ten minutes, not when it crosses a line, so you hear about it early. And put source-side bulk jobs on a shared calendar, so the pipeline owner knows a surge is coming before the pager does. In DMS, watch the source and target latency metrics separately; they point to different bottlenecks (check the troubleshooting guide for your version).

The usual response to “counts aren’t enough” is to compare a random sample of rows. It feels rigorous. It isn’t, and the maths is short. If N is the table size, n the sample size and k the number of corrupted rows, the chance of catching at least one is about 1 − (1 − n/N)^k.

In the example, 480 million rows and 120 bad ones (0.000025% of the table). A 1-million-row sample finds at least one bad row 22% of the time. A 10-million-row sample finds one 92% of the time, and costs ten times as much. Checksums over the whole table find it every time, because every row is counted in some bucket.

So I bucket the keys, compute cheap aggregates per bucket on both sides, and diff the results. Here’s a query that runs unchanged on Oracle and Redshift (untested; adapt types to your schema):

With 4,096 buckets, each holds about 117,000 rows. The 120 bad rows can touch at most 120 buckets, so the drill-down scans at most 14 million rows, 2.9% of the table. Two details matter more than the SQL:

The template I’d steal: each step has an action and a gate, and the gate is a number somebody can check. “Three clean reconciliation nights in a row” beats “looks good.” The T+7 row matters too. Keep the reverse path warm for a week, because mismatches that survive three clean nights tend to be the slow ones: month-end jobs, rare code paths, the table nobody remembered.

Counts are a smoke test. Land changes append-only and apply the latest per key. Watch the slope of lag and know your bulk jobs. Reconcile with bucketed checksums at a shared cut-off, and give every cutover step a gate that is a number.

How to Measure Product Success Without a Historical Baseline

#9706. Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon

The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware.

Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance.

You can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201).

The dashboard shows two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second:

Both tests start at context depth zero (n_depth=0). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput (avg_ts). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows.

We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh, the build and installation project behind llama.app. The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration.

The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M, Q8_0, other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16.

The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model.

Standard results use ///.jsonl. Workload sweeps use the same folder -tg.jsonl filename.

Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run.

#9705. Single-Node OpenShift on AWS via UPI: A Lean Setup for Labs & Training

Spinning up a Single-Node OpenShift (SNO) cluster on AWS for training or lab environments doesn't always require heavy Terraform or CloudFormation scaffolding. With User-Provisioned Infrastructure (UPI), you stay close to the actual mechanics and see every stage of the cluster coming up.

Because AWS AMIs do not support "Bootstrap-in-Place" installations, you briefly start with a temporary bootstrap instance before the master node takes over.

Always run the installer in a clean, empty directory—leftover hidden state files from earlier attempts can cause certificate or SNI mismatches. Also back up your install-config.yaml, as the installer removes it during setup:

(Add your Red Hat pull secret and SSH public key in the final two lines.)

To allow the ingress router and image registry to run on the single node, set mastersSchedulable to true before generating the Ignition files:

Because AWS EC2 User-Data is limited to 16 KB and the generated .ign files are larger, host bootstrap.ign and master.ign on your Nginx web server and pass small JSON pointer configs into EC2 User-Data:

Once the cluster is up, tighten your security group rules, remove the Ignition files from the web server (as they contain sensitive data), and raise the DNS TTL back up. For dynamic PVC provisioning, install Red Hat LVM Storage (LVMS) via a Subscription in the openshift-storage namespace.

For workshops and lab environments, the UPI route on AWS is great when you want visibility into bootstrap, cutover, and storage without hiding behind black-box automation.

For the full step-by-step walkthrough, check out the detailed guide in the repository: openshift_single_node_aws_upi_installation_guide.md.

#9703. The Last RAG Stack You'll Need: LangChain, ChromaDB, and Ollama on Your Own Hardware

Posted on Nov 27 • Originally published at mangodeveloper.com

I built my first RAG system two years ago. It cost me $400 in OpenAI API calls before I realized the team was querying the same 50 documents repeatedly. We were paying per token for retrieval over a static knowledge base. That's when it clicked-most RAG use cases don't need a frontier model in the cloud. They need a decent local model, a vector store that doesn't require a PhD to operate, and a framework that gets out of your way.

If you've ever wanted to run a production-grade retrieval-augmented chatbot on your own infrastructure-on a laptop, a homelab server, or a single VPS-this is the stack I'd recommend in 2025: LangChain for orchestration, ChromaDB for vector storage, and Ollama for the LLM runtime. No API keys. No per-token billing. No data leaving your network.

Let me walk you through building one end-to-end, including the parts most tutorials skip: chunking strategy, retrieval tuning, conversation memory, caching, monitoring, and Docker deployment.

For the LLM, I'll use Llama 3.1 8B through this guide. It's a solid default-small enough to run on a laptop, capable enough for most RAG tasks. If you have more RAM, swap in qwen2.5:14b or mistral-nemo and the code stays the same.

The ingestion pipeline (run separately) looks like:

Keep chroma_db/ on a persistent volume in production. Lose that directory and you'll re-embed your entire corpus, which for large datasets means hours of compute and a window where the chatbot returns zero results.

Install Ollama from ollama.com or via the install script:

I prefer nomic-embed-text over OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small for local setups. It's a 137M parameter model, runs in milliseconds on CPU, and produces embeddings competitive with proprietary options on standard benchmarks. If you need multilingual support, swap in bge-m3.

Embedding the same chunk twice is wasted compute. LangChain supports caching out of the box:

This is also useful during development. When you're iterating on prompts or chunking strategies, caching the LLM calls saves you from regenerating answers for unchanged contexts-which on a local 8B model still takes 5-10 seconds per query and adds up fast when you're running evals.

I've used all three in production. LangChain wins on developer ergonomics and the size of the integration ecosystem. LlamaIndex has better ingestion pipelines for complex document types and a more opinionated (in a good way) approach to retrieval. Haystack is overkill unless you're building a search product at scale.

A breakdown for a typical small-team deployment (5-20 users, ~10K documents):

Total: roughly $50/month plus your time. Compare this to per-seat pricing on hosted RAG services, which typically run $20-50/user/month. For a 10-person team, you're looking at $200-500/month vs $50/month. The break-even point is usually around 3-5 users.

The hidden cost is the ops burden. You're now responsible for uptime, updates, and incident response. If your team doesn't have bandwidth for that, the hosted option is worth the premium.

Local RAG has crossed the threshold from "interesting experiment" to "production-ready default" in the last year. The combination of LangChain's orchestration, ChromaDB's simplicity, and Ollama's model runtime gives you a stack that's private, predictable in cost, and fast enough for real users.

The hard part isn't the setup. It's the iteration-tuning chunk size, picking the right embedding model, deciding between semantic and hybrid search, and building the observability to know when things break. Start with the defaults in this article, ship it to your team, and refine based on actual usage. The first version will be 70% as good as it could be. That's enough to be useful, and the feedback loop will tell you what to fix next.

#9702. Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work.

With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos?

I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result.

I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API.

For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX says makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines.

The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened:

Each shot has a name and a prompt, and can have a seed, to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next:

A shot can also be trimmed, or have a caption drawn over it.

Making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames (to), and the shots after it start from its last frames (from). When a film builds up to a payoff (the moment everything was leading to), the payoff is the key shot. I found this order by trial and error, and made the seal film pose to pose, starting from iceberg.

The payoff is iceberg: the iceberg rolls over, and its wave drenches the seal. nap, the sleeping seal, ends on the first 9 frames of iceberg (to), so that the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same into the payoff. shake starts from the last 25 frames of iceberg (from): the dripping seal shakes off the water and flops down on the floe. The dream is made on its own, and a cut joins it to the rest.

On the diffusers side, three pipelines share the models of LTX-2.5. LTX2Pipeline makes the shots from their prompt alone, and LTX2ConditionPipeline makes the shots that start or end on frames of another shot. These two follow the two-stage distilled recipe of the model card: 8 steps, then the third pipeline, LTX2LatentUpsamplePipeline, upscales the latents ×2 before 3 final steps.

The diffusers pipelines do all of the generation. The film part is about 160 lines of Python on top: read the film file, order the shots so each keyframe exists before the shot that needs it, and cut the frames to hand over; then trim, caption, even out the sound and assemble the film. The code is in dacorvo/video-generation. The films I kept are in the dacorvo/video-generation bucket, with their JSON files: the seal, the fox, and the goat, which trims two of its shots and draws a caption over its payoff.

Out of the box, the model does not run on the NeuronCores: the transformer does not fit on one, and diffusers has no plan to split it. The first attempt that ran (the model card's pipeline, with the transformer split over 4 cores and a few patches) took about 5 min 20 s for a 10-second clip, and the NeuronCores were actually computing for only about 45 s of it. What's more, the target resolution was out of reach.

Getting there took three kinds of work: making the model run on the NeuronCores (requires tensor parallelism), splitting it over more of them (sequence parallelism), and making the host keep up with them.

Most of the fixes below are on the device, and that is where most of the effort went. The biggest end-to-end savings came from the host: the low-hanging fruit, since that is obviously where the waste was.

Three issues were never explained: the transformer compiled as one graph returned NaN at one size, the first shot that ends on keyframes was slow in each new process (even with every graph in the cache), and the latent upsampler fails to load next to the transformer, so it stays on the CPU.

Some of this is being fixed upstream. diffusers#15420 (open) fixes the LTX-2 pipelines, which would make the second workaround above unnecessary. diffusers#14725 (still open) brings tensor and context parallelism into one ParallelConfig, and a _tp_plan for LTX-2.5 is planned.

On the performance side, once the models are loaded, a 10-second 2048×1024 clip with sound takes 22 to 23 s. That rivals LTX's paid API, on half of the instance. A service would keep its processes up, as they take about 3 minutes to load the models, and 80 s for their first clip.

On the feature side, diffusers has what it takes to draft a movie. The shots come from prompts, and keep their subject from one shot to the next by starting or ending on frames of other shots. Takes differ by their seed, and the film file keeps the one I picked. Re-run with the same code and film file, and you get the same film back, byte for byte. A shot can also start from an image, such as a storyboard frame or a character sheet, which the condition pipeline takes the same way as frames (I did not try it in a film).

LTX calls LTX-2.5 a world model, with robotics as an emerging use. Robots, cars and drones learn from videos of what their cameras see, and a world model can make more of them, including events too rare or too risky to film. So I also tried it on real footage, with the same code: a shot can start from the first second of a real camera clip and invent what happens next. One frame was not enough, as the model cannot tell from it how fast things move.

Here is the head camera of a Fourier GR1-T2 humanoid robot (a clip from NVIDIA's GR1-100), looking down at a table. In the real 6-second clip, the robot's left hand picks an orange from a plate and drops it in a tray. The model only sees the first second of that clip (the hands raised, before anything moves) and invents the rest. What really happened, next to its invention:

Same scene, same pick: the model invents the grab on its own, and keeps the table, the hands and the fruit consistent with the real footage. More interesting are the events that did not happen. From the same second, with only the prompt changed, a person leans over and grabs the orange too, and the human hand and the robot hand carry it to the tray together. Five takes, with the real footage first:

The person's gestures and timing differ in each take, and the robot's arm adapts to them. That is the appeal for training: not one continuation of a clip, but a distribution of them, each reproducible from its film file and seed.

The robotics folder of the bucket has the five takes with their JSON files, and a second example from the front camera of a car in a snowstorm (Boreas), where the alternate event is slush thrown on the lens by a passing truck. Asked to make the car accelerate instead, the model kept its speed: the prompt does not override what the first second of footage already implies.

These videos follow prompts, not the robot's or car's commands: a training setup would need generation conditioned on those actions. For that, a team fine-tunes the pre-trained checkpoint of LTX-2.5 on the frames and actions of its own robots.

The Ferrari made it around the track, on half of its cylinders.

#9700. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. #9699. What breaks when your app scales to zero, and how to catch it

Posted on Nov 27 • Originally published at gregale.dev

Originally published on gregale.dev. I build Gregale, so read this as a vendor's page. Competitor details come from each vendor's own docs, linked in the post. This post was written with AI assistance.

When an app scales to zero, whatever it kept only on its own machine is lost, such as files written to local disk or /tmp and sessions held in memory, and timers or background loops meant to run between requests stop. Anything in a database, in object storage or in the platform's crons and queues keeps working, because it lives outside the instance. On Gregale, every wake starts from the same snapshot and parking discards the instance's local state, so Gregale looks for the usual mistakes: it refuses stateful base images and VOLUME directives when it accepts a deploy, and records an audit row the first time an app writes to a database-shaped directory such as /data or /var/lib/postgresql. These stateless contract checks are generally available on every plan.

By default the snapshot is taken from the deployment, right after the app becomes ready, not from the instance that parked. So every wake starts from the same state, whatever the last instance did, and two instances restored at once start from the same memory. Two settings change what is in that memory; see What goes into the snapshot.

Only the first and last rows are things Gregale checks for you. The others are design choices; the table is the list to review before you deploy.

At deploy. Gregale rejects a stateful base image when it accepts the deployment, with stateless_only_violation and HTTP 422: postgres:16, mysql:8, redis:7, mongo:7, mariadb, cockroach, cassandra, clickhouse and the rest. A source tarball with a VOLUME directive, or with top-level data/ or db/ directories, is rejected for the same reason.

At runtime. Gregale watches the state-shaped directories in every instance: data/ and db/ under the app's working directory, plus /data, /db and /var/lib/postgresql, /var/lib/mysql, /var/lib/redis and the data directories of other databases. The first write to each file there records one stateless.advisory audit row. The check is advisory: the app keeps running, and the row is your signal that the data will not survive the next park.

The first command lists recent rows; the second streams them live while you exercise the app. Each file is reported once per instance, and an instance reports at most 256 files.

Before you sign up. Will it run here? reads a public GitHub repository and says whether it would run on Gregale, without building or deploying anything.

Priming. Just before the snapshot is taken, Gregale sends up to 20 GET requests to the app's health check path, or to / when it declares none, so the snapshot holds a runtime that has already loaded and connected. Those requests run your code. If that path writes data, sends mail or calls a paid API, it does so up to 20 times per deploy. Declare a harmless warm-up path instead:

Warm snapshots. Pro and Scale apps can opt in to a second snapshot, taken when an instance parks after it has served a few requests. It is reused by every later wake and every instance until the next deploy, and it carries whatever those first requests left in memory: sessions, caches, rate-limit counters, per-user data and files under /tmp. An app that keeps per-user state in memory must not use it. Apps created before 2026-11-10 on Pro or Scale were opted in by default; turn it off with:

A connection opened at startup is captured in the snapshot, so a restored instance must reopen it. Declare an after_restore hook in gregale.yaml:

After a restore, and after it has repaired the guest's clock and entropy, Gregale sends one POST to that path on the app's loopback listener. A 2xx answer lets the instance serve; a timeout or any other status discards it and Gregale cold-boots a fresh one instead. The timeout is 500 ms by default and at most 2 seconds. Check for a loopback peer and the X-Faas-After-Restore: 1 header in the handler: Gregale strips inbound x-faas-* headers at its public proxy, so a public caller cannot fake that marker. To close the connection before the snapshot is taken instead, add a before_checkpoint hook the same way. Redeploy after changing either: existing snapshots keep the configuration of the deployment that made them.

A Node or Python function declares the same thing as hooks in its handler file: init, beforeSnapshot and afterRestore (before_snapshot and after_restore in Python).

The writable layer on each instance is real disk, bounded by your plan's ephemeral disk ceiling, and writes to it are rate limited per plan:

Each applies after a one-time burst of 256 MiB and 20,000 operations. Use the disk for work that ends with the request, such as unpacking an archive or rendering a file before you upload it.

None of them keeps local files once the instance, execution environment or dyno is gone, and neither does Gregale. What Gregale adds is catching the mistake: at deploy for the clear cases, and with an audit row the first time a running app writes where it looks like it expects data to last.

Sources, checked 2026-11-27: Cloud Run container runtime contract, Lambda ephemeral storage, Heroku dynos.

Stateless contract checks are generally available on every plan, Free included, and paused seconds are not billed on any plan. See Gregale pricing, Storage and How scaling to zero works.

Anything kept only on the instance: files written to local disk or /tmp, sessions and caches held in memory, and timers meant to run between requests. Data in a database, object storage or the platform’s crons and queues is kept.

How does Gregale warn me that my app writes data it will lose?

It rejects stateful base images such as postgres:16 and VOLUME directives at deploy with stateless_only_violation, and records a stateless.advisory audit row the first time an app writes to a database-shaped directory such as /data or /var/lib/postgresql.

How do I reconnect to my database after a snapshot restore?

Declare an after_restore hook in gregale.yaml. Gregale sends one POST to that path on the app’s loopback listener after repairing the clock and entropy; a 2xx answer lets the instance serve, anything else falls back to a cold boot.

Can a snapshot carry one user’s data into other instances?

Only if you opt in to warm snapshots on Pro or Scale, or your app was created there before 2026-11-10. A warm snapshot is taken after an instance has served a few requests and keeps what they left in memory, so apps with per-user state in memory should turn it off with --no-warm-snapshot.

Not while it is paused. About a second after the last request, with nothing in flight, Gregale pauses the VM in memory, and paused seconds are not billed. An app that keeps itself busy with timers keeps running and is billed while it works.

#9696. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.

To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.

When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows).

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab.

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9680. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

Buy Now Pay Later services let you split a purchase into installments — typically four payments over six weeks (Afterpay, Klarna "Pay in 4") or monthly payments over 3-36 months (Affirm, Klarna financing). The checkout process is seamless: enter your name and email, get instantly approved, and walk away with your purchase having paid only the first installment.

BNPL providers make money in two ways. First, they charge merchants 4-8% of each transaction — significantly more than the 2-3% credit card processing fee. Merchants accept this because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50%. Second, some providers charge interest on longer-term plans, and nearly all charge late fees when you miss a payment.

The "interest-free" label on short-term plans deserves scrutiny. While you may not pay interest, the behavioral cost is substantial. Research from multiple financial studies shows that BNPL users spend 30-50% more per transaction than they would with cash or debit. The psychological separation of the purchase from the full payment removes the natural spending brake that keeps budgets in check.

The financial industry has known for decades that separating the moment of purchase from the moment of payment increases spending. Credit cards exploit this. BNPL takes it further by making the payment feel even smaller — "just four easy payments of $37.50" feels dramatically different from "$150" even though it is the same amount.

A 2026 survey found that 43% of BNPL users have missed at least one payment. Among those who missed payments, the average person missed three or more over the prior year. Late fees compound quickly — four missed $8 Afterpay fees on a $200 purchase adds $32, effectively creating a 16% surcharge on what was supposed to be interest-free.

The credit score impact is evolving rapidly. As recently as 2022, most BNPL activity was invisible to credit bureaus. That has changed. Affirm now reports all payment activity to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna reports financing plans to all three bureaus. On-time BNPL payments may slightly help your score, but missed payments can drop it significantly — and the damage lasts up to seven years.

For anyone pursuing financial independence, BNPL represents the opposite of the FI mindset. FI is built on intentional spending, high savings rates, and letting compound growth work in your favor. BNPL encourages impulsive spending, fragments your cash flow, and creates obligations that reduce your ability to invest.

There is exactly one scenario where BNPL is financially rational: a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you would have paid the full price regardless. For example, you need a new dishwasher, you have the $800 in savings, and the retailer offers four interest-free payments. You keep your $800 invested for six more weeks while paying in installments. The benefit is tiny — a few dollars of investment returns — but the cost is genuinely zero if you make every payment on time.

Outside this narrow scenario, BNPL is almost always a worse choice than the alternatives.

The financial independence community is nearly unanimous: BNPL is a trap disguised as convenience. The entire BNPL business model depends on you spending more than you planned. If you were going to buy the item anyway and you have the cash, just buy it. If you do not have the cash, that is your budget telling you something important.

The question to ask before any BNPL checkout: "Would I buy this right now if I had to pay the full price in cash today?" If the answer is no, BNPL is not helping you afford something — it is helping you overspend. If the answer is yes, just pay cash and skip the installment tracking, the payment reminders, and the risk of a missed payment damaging your credit.

For those building toward financial independence, every dollar matters. The 30-50% spending increase that BNPL encourages directly reduces your savings rate — the single most important variable in determining how quickly you reach FI.

The average ChooseFI listener saves $24,000+ with an expert student loan plan.

Trusted by Brad Barrett, Co-founder and Host, ChooseFI

Mortgage lenders are increasingly scrutinizing BNPL obligations during the underwriting process. Multiple active BNPL plans — even if interest-free — show up as recurring liabilities and can affect your debt-to-income ratio. If you are planning to apply for a mortgage or auto loan in the next 6-12 months, pay off all BNPL balances and avoid opening new ones. Lenders view fragmented installment obligations as a sign of cash flow stress, even if you have never missed a payment.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Affirm is a legitimate, publicly traded company (AFRM on NASDAQ). It is safe in the sense that it will not steal your money or identity. However, being legitimate does not mean it is a good financial decision. Affirm's interest rates range from 0-36% APR depending on creditworthiness, and the company reports all payment activity to credit bureaus.

Increasingly, yes. Affirm reports to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna financing plans report to all three bureaus. On-time payments may help slightly, but a single missed payment can significantly damage your score and remains on your report for up to seven years.

Afterpay charges an $8 late fee per missed payment, capped at 25% of the order value. After multiple missed payments, your account is suspended, the balance is sent to collections, and the delinquency is reported to Equifax. Collections accounts damage your credit score severely and remain for seven years.

Klarna's "Pay in 4" plan is interest-free with no late fees, but your account may be suspended for missed payments. Klarna's longer-term financing plans charge 7.99-33.99% APR, involve a hard credit pull, and report to all three credit bureaus. Read the terms carefully — the word "Klarna" covers very different products.

It is possible but unlikely for most people. Research consistently shows that BNPL increases spending by 30-50% per transaction. If you have the discipline to use BNPL only on planned, budgeted purchases at 0% interest — and never miss a payment — the financial harm is minimal. But for most users, the behavioral cost exceeds any convenience benefit.

Because it works — for the store. Merchants pay BNPL providers 4-8% of each transaction (vs 2-3% for credit cards) because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50% and reduces cart abandonment by 20-30%. The merchant is paying for you to spend more. That should tell you who this arrangement benefits.

Buy Now Pay Later is a marketing innovation designed to make you spend more — and the data confirms it works. BNPL users spend 30-50% more per transaction, 43% miss payments, and the credit reporting implications are growing. The only responsible use case is a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you already have the cash. For everyone else, especially those pursuing financial independence, BNPL is a detour in the wrong direction. Pay with cash, invest the difference, and let compound growth work for you instead of against you.

#9676. 20 Repos, 713K Stars: The Open Source Tools That Build, Tune and Run Language Models

Keep digging. Every project here on textmining.tech is real, open source, and pulled straight from GitHub.

Keep digging. Every project here on textmining.tech is real, open source, and pulled straight from GitHub.

Keep digging. Every project here on textmining.tech is real, open source, and pulled straight from GitHub.

huggingface/transformers is the most-starred repo in the whole directory, at 169.4K. This week it added 100 stars. OpenVINO, Intel's inference toolkit, has 12.8K stars and added 1.3K, thirteen times as many. That gap says where the work is now. Most teams no longer write a model from scratch. They pick one that already exists, tune it on their own data, and then fight to make it run fast and cheap on the hardware they have.

Every repo below comes from TextMining.Tech, HackerNoon's directory of 7,075 open source text mining tools, libraries and frameworks with at least 100 stars each. They're grouped by job: define the model, train or fine-tune it, then run it.

This is part 2 of a four-part series. Part 1 covered the tools that read documents, retrieve context and teach you to build. Speech and voice come next.

These repos hold the models themselves, or the code and data that define them. transformers is the hub most of the others plug into; the rest are model families built for a language, a domain or a different way of answering.

The model-definition framework for text, vision, audio and multimodal models, for inference and training

Non-autoregressive engine that makes typed choice, score and yes/no decisions over text in one forward pass, in 100+ languages

Microsoft's large-scale self-supervised pre-training across tasks, languages and modalities

Ready-to-use datasets for AI models, with tools to load and transform them

Alibaba Cloud's official repo for the original Qwen chat and pretrained models

Open source financial LLMs, with trained models released on Hugging Face

Chinese LLaMA and Alpaca models, with local CPU and GPU training and deployment

laya added nearly three times as many stars as transformers this week, from a base a fifth the size.

Once you have a base model, these repos adapt it to your data or train new ones at scale. They range from a one-stop fine-tuning toolkit to the distributed systems behind frontier-scale training, plus two 2023-era projects that taught a generation how instruction tuning works.

Unified, efficient fine-tuning for 100+ LLMs and vision-language models (ACL 2024)

Distributed compute engine with libraries for scaling training and other ML workloads

Community-built chat assistant project, including its crowd-sourced training data

Code and data generation for training Stanford's Alpaca instruction-tuned models

An open book on the engineering of training and running large models

NVIDIA's research code for training transformer models at scale

White Circle's framework for training large language and multimodal models

halo is the smallest repo in this series so far, and it added more stars this week than anything else in this group.

A tuned model is only useful once it answers requests. These repos run models locally, compile them for phones and browsers, wire them into apps, and watch what they do in production.

Self-hosted engine that runs LLMs, vision, voice, image and video models on any hardware, no GPU required

AI engineering platform with a gateway, agent observability, evals and prompt management, built on OpenTelemetry

Vercel's AI SDK for building AI-powered apps and agents in TypeScript

Universal LLM deployment engine that uses ML compilation to target many devices

High-performance LLM inference that runs inside the browser

Toolkit for optimizing and deploying AI inference

The smallest repo in this group gained the most: OpenVINO's 1.3K stars this week topped the whole Natural Language Processing category.

All numbers come from the TextMining.Tech snapshot of Nov 26, 2026. The directory tracks open source GitHub repos with at least 100 stars, excludes archived repos and forks, and refreshes daily. We started from the top repos in the Language Models and Natural Language Processing categories and kept the ones that define, train or run models. "Added this week" is the directory's own weekly star count. Stars will have moved by the time you read this, so each repo name links to its live directory page.

Part 3 is speech and voice. VoiceStudio, a fully local voice cloning, dubbing and transcription suite, added 4.9K stars this week, more than all 20 repos in this list combined.

Until then, browse the full categories on TextMining.Tech:

Or open the full directory of 7,075 repos, sort by "Trending this week", and see what's climbing before it makes the next list. Built something that belongs here? Once it passes 100 stars, it's in.

#9675. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

In this article, we have taken a look at some of the biggest benefits associated with using sellfy for eCommerce. Once you compare these benefits to what you get with other platforms such as Shopify, you should find that it is worth your time to consider sellfy for your business. #9671. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing.

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

Sounds like you're biased for Grammarly. Not really that informative if you're already leaning towards one to begin with. Still, it was an interesting read. Tell me, do you use Grammarly with your day-to-day writing/blogging?

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. It doesn't matter that you never agreed to be a beta tester for them; you get to do it anyway.- Pro Writing Aid actually counts the occurrences of words in your document and tells you when a word has been overused compared to published literature. Grammarly, on the other hand, seems hell-bent to remove certain words that it has deemed overused from the language, whether or not they're actually overused in your document.- Grammarly's Clarity function is simply horrible. It mangles sentences and changes their meaning. Sometimes the result of its suggestion is unintelligible garbage.- Grammarly allows you to turn off some checks, but not all of them. Unfortunately, the ones you cannot turn off are some of the most irritating (such as that horrible "Clarity"). On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.
